questions.stem: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other at a point. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.explanation: For perpendicular forces the resultant is the hypotenuse: $R = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \text{N}$. This is the familiar 3–4–5 triangle.

distractorRationale.a: Subtracted the forces, which is the resultant only when they act in exactly opposite directions
distractorRationale.c: Added the forces arithmetically, which is the resultant only when they act in the same direction
distractorRationale.d: Multiplied the two forces instead of combining them as vectors

questions.stem: The equilibrant of a system of forces is a single force which is

options.text: equal in magnitude and direction to the resultant
equal in magnitude to the resultant but opposite in direction
half the magnitude of the resultant

questions.explanation: To hold a system at rest you must exactly cancel the resultant, which requires a force of the same size acting the opposite way. Adding the equilibrant to the original forces gives zero resultant, so the body stays in equilibrium.

distractorRationale.a: That would double the resultant rather than cancel it
distractorRationale.c: Half the resultant leaves half of it uncancelled, so the body would still accelerate
distractorRationale.d: A perpendicular force cannot cancel the resultant; it only changes its direction

questions.stem: For a rigid body acted upon by several coplanar forces to be in equilibrium, it is necessary that

options.text: the sum of the forces is zero only
the sum of the moments about any point is zero only
both the vector sum of the forces and the sum of the moments about any point are zero
all the forces act through the same point

questions.explanation: Zero resultant force prevents the body from accelerating in a straight line, and zero total moment prevents it from rotating. Both are required: two equal opposite forces along different lines form a couple, which gives zero resultant force yet still spins the body.

distractorRationale.a: Insufficient — a couple satisfies this yet still rotates the body
distractorRationale.b: Insufficient — the body could have zero net moment and still be accelerating in a straight line
distractorRationale.d: Concurrency is not required; forces on a beam act at different points and can still balance

questions.stem: Two forces of 6.0 N and 8.0 N act at right angles to each other at a point. Calculate the magnitude of their resultant. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: $R = \sqrt{6.0^2 + 8.0^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\ \text{N}$. This is the 3–4–5 triangle scaled by a factor of 2, so recognising the pattern gives the answer immediately.

questions.stem: A force of 50 N acts at 60° to the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal component. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: The horizontal component uses the cosine of the angle measured from the horizontal: $F_x = F\cos 60^{\circ} = 50 \times 0.5 = 25\ \text{N}$. Using sin 60° instead would give 43.3 N, which is the vertical component.

questions.stem: A boy pulls a box with a force of 12 N eastwards while a girl pulls the same box with a force of 5 N northwards. The single force that would produce the same effect has magnitude
questions.explanation: East and north are perpendicular, so $R = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13\ \text{N}$. The 5–12–13 triangle appears often in exam questions.

distractorRationale.a: Subtracted the forces as if they were opposite in direction
distractorRationale.c: Added the magnitudes as if the forces were along the same line
distractorRationale.d: Multiplied the two magnitudes together

questions.stem: Two forces of 7 N and 4 N act at a point. The greatest and least possible values of their resultant are respectively
questions.explanation: The resultant is largest when the forces act in the same direction, giving $7 + 4 = 11\ \text{N}$, and smallest when they oppose each other, giving $7 - 4 = 3\ \text{N}$. Any value between 3 N and 11 N is possible at some intermediate angle.

distractorRationale.b: A zero resultant would need the two forces to be equal in magnitude, which they are not
distractorRationale.c: Multiplied the forces rather than adding them
distractorRationale.d: Quoted the perpendicular resultant √(49+16) = 8.06 N, which is one particular case rather than the maximum

questions.stem: A crate of weight 500 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Calculate the component of its weight acting down the plane. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: The component of weight along a plane inclined at angle θ is $W\sin\theta = 500 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 500 \times 0.5 = 250\ \text{N}$. The perpendicular component, equal to the normal reaction on a smooth plane, is $500\cos 30^{\circ} = 433\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: A particle is acted upon by a force of 10 N due east and a force of 10 N due north. A third force keeps the particle in equilibrium. Calculate the magnitude of this third force. Give your answer in newtons, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The resultant of the two given forces is $\sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{200} = 14.14\ \text{N}$ directed north-east. The third force must be the equilibrant: the same magnitude, $14.14\ \text{N}$, but directed south-west.

questions.stem: Two forces, each of magnitude 10 N, act at a point with an angle of 120° between them. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.explanation: Use $R = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos\theta}$ with $\cos 120^{\circ} = -0.5$: $R = \sqrt{100 + 100 + 2(100)(-0.5)} = \sqrt{200 - 100} = \sqrt{100} = 10\ \text{N}$. Equal forces at 120° always give a resultant equal to one of them.

distractorRationale.a: Zero resultant would require an angle of 180°, that is directly opposed forces
distractorRationale.c: This is √300, obtained by using cos 60° = +0.5 instead of cos 120° = −0.5
distractorRationale.d: This assumes the forces are in the same direction, which corresponds to an angle of 0°

questions.stem: If two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at an angle of 90° to each other, what is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.explanation: To find the resultant of two perpendicular forces, we can use the Pythagorean theorem. The resultant R = √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 N.

distractorRationale.a: This is a common miscalculation, perhaps confusing the smaller force with the resultant.
distractorRationale.c: This option underestimates the resultant by not considering both forces adequately.
distractorRationale.d: This option significantly underestimates the resultant, possibly by misunderstanding vector addition.
